---
title: "SNP vs Microhaplotypes"
---

## TL;DR

::: {.callout-tip}
A **SNP** is a single biallelic locus. A **microhaplotype (MH) block**
is a short genomic window (~2–20 phased SNPs) treated as a single
multi-allelic locus. The MH representation typically has **more
distinct alleles per locus** and **larger expected effect sizes**, so
it can capture LD with causal variants that any one SNP misses — at the
cost of needing phased read data and a block-discovery step.
:::

## Information content per locus

A biallelic SNP carries at most $\log_2 3 \approx 1.58$ bits of
information per individual (3 genotype states: 0/1/2). A MH block of
$k$ phased SNPs has up to $2^k$ distinct haplotypes — though in
practice LD collapses this to a much smaller observed set. For the
demo dataset with $k = 2$, each block has up to 4 observed haplotype
combinations per strand, so each individual at each block carries
$\log_2 \binom{4 + 1}{2} \approx 3.3$ bits.

The practical consequence: a 100-SNP set arranged into 50 MH blocks
($k = 2$) typically tags **more genetic variance** than the same 100
SNPs treated individually, because the MH encoding preserves cis-LD
that the per-SNP encoding drops.

## The encoding trade-off

| Aspect | SNP | Microhaplotypes |
|---|---|---|
| Number of loci | $p$ | $n_{\text{blocks}} = p / k$ |
| Alleles per locus | 2 | up to $2^k$ |
| Design matrix width | $p$ | $\sum_b (n_{\text{alleles},b} - 1)$ |
| Per-locus effect size $|\beta|$ | smaller (effect split across SNPs in LD) | larger (aggregated across cis-SNPs) |
| Robustness to genotyping error | one mis-call → wrong dosage at one SNP | one mis-call → wrong haplotype id for the whole block |
| Need phasing? | no | yes |
| LD pruning needed? | yes (in dense panels) | no — within-block LD is what makes the block informative |

For the columns of `masbayes`'s $W_{\alpha h}$ matrix, each MH block
contributes $n_{\text{alleles},b} - 1$ columns (one allele is the
dummy-encoded reference); see
[Microhaplotypes](../input-data/microhaplotypes.qmd#schema).

## Why MH-GBLUP can beat SNP-GBLUP

Both methods compute $\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{W}^\top / c$ for
some centring of $\mathbf{W}$ and a trace-scaling constant $c$ (see the
[VanRaden Method 1 formula](gblup-gwablup.qmd#eq-grm-snp)). The kernels differ
because the column space of $\mathbf{W}_{\text{SNP}}$ is **strictly
smaller** than that of $\mathbf{W}_{\text{MH}}$ when blocks contain
$k \geq 2$ SNPs in tight LD — the MH encoding preserves the
interaction (linkage phase) between within-block SNPs that the
additive SNP coding cannot represent.

The gain is concentrated at causal variants in LD with multiple SNPs in
the panel. For a polygenic infinitesimal architecture spread evenly
across all SNPs, the two kernels converge.

## When microhaplotypes lose

1. **Genotyping noise.** A single mis-called SNP within a block
   flips the whole-block haplotype id, propagating a small error into
   a larger one. SNP-GBLUP is less sensitive: one bad SNP perturbs
   one column of $\mathbf{W}$.
2. **No phased reads available.** MH calling requires phase
   information. Imputation can recover phase from population reference
   panels but adds an error layer.
3. **Cross-population transfer with different LD patterns.** Block
   definitions discovered in population A may not be informative in
   population B; SNP-GBLUP transfers slightly worse but more
   predictably.
4. **Small training samples ($n < 200$).** The $W_{\alpha h}$ design
   matrix is wider than the SNP one for the same $p$ raw markers, so
   the $p/n$ ratio is worse. Variance estimation gets noisier.

## When to use which

| Situation | Pick |
|---|---|
| Phased reads available, polygenic + a few QTL | MH (better LD coverage) |
| Phased reads available, infinitesimal architecture | SNP and MH perform similarly; SNP simpler |
| No phasing infrastructure | SNP |
| Genotyping error rate > 1% per SNP | SNP |
| Cross-population prediction with shared causal variants | MH (more transferable signal) |
| Cross-population with population-specific LD | SNP (more predictable transfer) |
